Use only if clearly needed; limited data, no strong evidence of harm
Small amounts in milk; generally considered compatible
Reduce dose in renal impairment based on serum creatinine
Signs of thrombosis; vision changes on long-term use
summary: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic that stabilizes clots by blocking plasminogen activation. It is used to reduce bleeding - in heavy menstrual bleeding, dental procedures in hemophilia, trauma, and surgical hemorrhage. Key cautions are thromboembolism risk and the need for renal dose adjustment; it is contraindicated in active thromboembolic disease.
indications: Reduction/prevention of hemorrhage during and after tooth extraction in patients with hemophilia (IV)
Cyclic heavy menstrual bleeding (oral, where labeled)
Other off-label: trauma hemorrhage, surgical and obstetric bleeding

dosage.d: 10 mg/kg actual body weight IV immediately before extraction, then 10 mg/kg 3-4 times daily
dosage.n: For 2 to 8 days; infuse no faster than 1 mL/min

dosage.d: 1300 mg (two 650 mg tablets) three times daily
Reduce dose by serum creatinine: SCr 1.36-2.83 mg/dL give 10 mg/kg twice daily; 2.83-5.66 mg/dL give 10 mg/kg daily; >5.66 mg/dL give 10 mg/kg every 48 h or 5 mg/kg daily

admin: IV: infuse no more than 1 mL/minute to avoid hypotension
Oral tablets swallowed whole, not chewed or crushed
Do not mix IV tranexamic acid with blood products or penicillin in the same line
moa: A synthetic lysine derivative that competitively binds to the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, blocking its activation to plasmin. This prevents fibrin clot breakdown (fibrinolysis), stabilizing clots and reducing bleeding.

relative: Hematuria of upper urinary tract origin (clot retention)

preg: Use only if clearly needed. Tranexamic acid crosses the placenta; available data have not demonstrated a clear increase in malformations, but data are limited. Used in obstetric hemorrhage (e.g., postpartum) where benefit outweighs risk.
lact: Excreted into breast milk at about 1% of maternal serum concentration; antifibrinolytic effect in the infant is considered unlikely. Generally compatible.
renal: Dose reduction is required in renal impairment because the drug is renally excreted. Adjust dose and/or frequency according to serum creatinine.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment generally required; metabolism is minimal.

major: Factor IX complex / anti-inhibitor coagulant concentrates (increased thrombosis risk)
moderate: Tretinoin (in acute promyelocytic leukemia - thrombotic risk)

serious: Venous and arterial thromboembolism (DVT, PE, stroke, MI)

monitoring: Visual acuity and color vision on prolonged use
Blood pressure during IV infusion (avoid rapid infusion)
counsel: Report leg swelling/pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, or sudden vision changes immediately
For menstrual use, do not exceed 5 days per cycle
Tell your doctor if you use hormonal contraceptives or have had blood clots
Report any change in color vision during long-term therapy
pk: Antifibrinolytic effect within ~1 hour (oral); rapid with IV
Approximately 2-3 hours (elimination); antifibrinolytic effect in tissue longer
Hemostatic effect persists several hours; dose 2-4 times daily
Store at 20-25 C; protect from freezing (injection)
pearls: About 10x more potent than aminocaproic acid
Most effective when given early in bleeding (e.g., CRASH-2: within 3 hours of trauma)
Renally cleared - always check renal function before dosing
Avoid in subarachnoid hemorrhage outside specialist protocols
missed: For scheduled (e.g., menstrual) dosing, take the missed dose when remembered unless it is near the next dose; do not double up. For procedural/IV regimens, follow the clinician's instructions.
overdose: Overdose may cause hypotension (with rapid IV), nausea/vomiting, dizziness, and possibly thromboembolic events or seizures. Management is supportive; maintain hydration to promote renal excretion. No specific antidote.
